newsitem.title: UK: Palladium soars as Russia delays sales further.
newsitem.headline: Palladium soars as Russia delays sales further.

text.p: Speculation over how much more the price of palladium, a rare metal used in electronics and cars, can rise heated up on Wednesday on potential new delays in Russian supplies.

The price for spot metal has already risen by 40 percent since its 43-month low of $114.25 late last November to $159.50/ounce on Wednesday -- a 21-month high -- and more gains were on the cards while Russia, the world's biggest exporter, stayed off the market, dealers and analysts said.

"Let's face it. It is a very remarkable situation in which the world's largest supplier in effect goes to sleep for five months. In a sense perhaps prices should be much higher," said Tony Warwick-Ching, precious metals consultant at CRU International.
The big unknown is what price level would tempt hedge funds to sell the hefty long positions they have built over the past months.

The most involved is the U.S.-based Tiger Management with $8.5 billion under control. Julian Robertson who runs the fund said prices could rise to $200-$300 before substitution to other metals could occur.

Problems arose in December when Russia postponed talks with Japan, the biggest palladium importer which took 77.41 tonnes in 1996, to negotiate sale contracts for 1997, citing domestic budget complications.

But a chain of bureaucratic and political snags delayed talks for four months. The Russians have yet to address which ministry has the power to set export quotas in platinum group metals for the state agency Almaz.

The market received a further chill this week when a Russian trade official said there would be no shipments in April and possibly none in May. It was not known when the talks with Japan might start, he said.
Palladium is used as catalytic converters for cleaning up car exhausts. But its main use is in electronics, which accounts for 60 percent of Japan's palladium imports.
Japanese buyers have tapped European, mainly Swiss, and South African sources for short-term needs, and January import figures even show an increase on last year.

The United States bought large quantities in November and December, possibly anticipating the problem, and some of that material should be in the market. Some Russian metal may also have leaked out, analysts said.

But availability may be drying up now. "I suspect increases in price and lease rates is very much that there is less of that metal available for purchase and for leasing that there was earlier in the year," one analyst said.
One-month lease rates soared to 10 percent in Tokyo on Wednesday from about three earlier this year as traders scramble to borrow palladium to cover their immediate requirements.

While analysts expect prices to remain at least steady for the time being, the large speculative involvement built over the last few months suggests any news of Russians selling could produce a market collapse at a swoop.
"Anybody speculating in that way must be very conscious that when Russians come back into the market, that may have a very negative impact on the price," said another dealer.

In contrast, Japanee speculators on the Tokyo palladium futures market (Tocom) have sold the metal short -- selling metal they do not yet own on the basis that its price will fall when Russia begins to export allowing them to make a profit.
This has also pushed up the cost of borrowing palladium to cover these short positions making the gamble more expensive.
"The situation in the palladium market is now becoming quite serious," one Tokyo bullion house official said. "We will be forced to buy in the spot market."
